t: Secularism seeks to conduct human affairs on naturalistic considerations and is most commonly understood as the separation of religion from civil affairs and the state; it is concerned with minimising the role of religion rather than disproving it, and may be hostile, neutral or hospitable to religion.

The French, Turkish, American and Indian models differ greatly: the American emphasis falls on avoiding an established religion and on freedom of belief, the French model is interventionist, and the Indian model combines equality of citizens before the law with some separation.

The word was coined in 1851 by George Holyoake, who found “atheism” too aggravating and wanted a term that allowed cooperation with believers, but its origins have been traced to the Bible itself and through Christian history.
dyk: George Holyoake, who used the word “secularism” in its modern sense in 1851, did so because he found “atheism” too aggravating; he wanted a stance that did not necessarily reject religion and so allowed cooperation with believers.
ev: Roger Williams founds the Providence Plantations in present-day Rhode Island as a settlement with total freedom of religion
George Holyoake uses the word secularism in its modern sense in Britain
A French law enshrines laïcité, the principle of strict separation
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk comes to power and Turkish secularism, laiklik, becomes a state ideology under Kemalism
India becomes a secular state on achieving independence
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights protects freedom of religion in international law
John Rawls publishes A Theory of Justice, whose line of work leads many political theorists to prefer overlapping consensus to secularism

f.thinkers: George Holyoake, the British agnostic writer who used the word in its modern sense in 1851; Roger Williams, founder of the Providence Plantations in 1636; John Locke, whose ideas Thomas Jefferson and James Madison built into the government of the United States; Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who made laiklik a state ideology in Turkey; Mahatma Gandhi, who supported pluralist secularism in India; John Rawls, whose overlapping consensus replaced the word among political theorists; Rajeev Bhargava, author of the chapter “Political secularism”
f.texts: John Rawls’s A Theory of Justice (1971) and Political Liberalism (1993); Rajeev Bhargava’s chapter “Political secularism” in The Oxford Handbook of Political Theory; the French law of 1905 that established laïcité; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
f.ideas: the separation of church and state; legal equality between people of different religions; state supremacy of the rule of law over canon law and religious diktat; freedom of thought and of belief, with the government able to enforce how people act but not what they believe; religious tolerance; reason as a virtue; freedom from religion as an extension of freedom of religion; ethics that do not depend on religious or supernatural concepts
f.today: constitutionally secular states include the United States, France, Turkey, India, Mexico and South Korea, though none has an identical form of governance with respect to religion; organisations such as the National Secular Society in the UK and the Center for Inquiry in the United States campaign for it; Rajeev Bhargava opens his chapter with the sentence “Secularism is a beleaguered doctrine”
